basics.title: Start with your token's purpose
basics.body: Choose a recognizable name and decide who should control the supply. Names describe the token; its saved rules determine what the owner and holders can do.
basics.example: A studio could issue StudioCredits for its rewards programme.

policy.title: Choose a starting policy
policy.body: A policy fills in supply amounts and permissions together. Compare the proposed changes before applying an example, then review every rule you customize.
policy.example: Choose fixed supply for a one-time issue, or owner-managed supply for later rewards.

fixed-policy.title: Fixed supply example
fixed-policy.body: This example creates 1,000 tokens and locks the maximum at 1,000. It disables additional issuer actions, their administrators and later-change allowances; ordinary transfers remain available.
fixed-policy.example: Issue 1,000 credits once, with no authority to mint more.
fixed-policy.consequence: Marketplace sales and direct purchases cannot be enabled under these example rules.

owner-policy.title: Owner-managed example
owner-policy.body: This example starts with 1,000 tokens and a permanent 10,000-token cap. The owner may mint, burn their own tokens, and pause or resume transfers. Other issuer powers and rule changes are disabled.
owner-policy.example: The owner can issue another 100 reward tokens while staying below the cap.

name.title: Token name
name.body: The display name helps people recognize your token. It does not prove ownership or make the token unique; the confirmed token identifier distinguishes it from other tokens. Both names are required. Use at least 3 characters without spaces, within 25 UTF-8 bytes; multibyte characters leave room for fewer characters.
name.example: StudioCredit is a name; two different tokens could use it.

plural.title: Plural name
plural.body: Choose the name clients should use when displaying more than one token. This changes the wording, not the number of tokens or their value. A plural name is required, even when it is the same as the singular name.

decimals.title: Decimal places
decimals.body: Choose how finely a token can be divided. Amount fields let you choose tokens or base units. Precision determines the smallest unit those amounts can represent.
decimals.example: With 2 decimal places, 1 token contains 100 smallest units and 1.25 tokens is valid.

description.title: Token description
description.body: Explain what the token is intended for in plain language. The description helps readers understand your plan; permissions and supply settings enforce the actual policy.
description.example: Credits awarded for participating in studio workshops.

capitalization.title: Name capitalization
capitalization.body: This is a display convention that clients can use when showing token names. It does not change the token identifier, create a translation, or affect balances.
capitalization.example: A client can use a capitalized name such as StudioCredit.

localizations.title: Names in other languages
localizations.body: Add one set of singular and plural names for each language you need. All translations describe the same token and share the same supply.
localizations.example: English: Point and Points. Polish: Punkt and Punkty.

initial.title: Initial supply
initial.body: These tokens are created when registration succeeds. They go to the default new-token recipient; if no default is configured, the contract owner receives the initial supply.
initial.example: An initial supply of 1,000 creates 1,000 tokens, not 1,000 DASH.

maximum.title: Maximum outstanding supply
maximum.body: This limits how many tokens may exist at once. Burning tokens frees capacity for future minting if minting is allowed. Review who may change this maximum.
maximum.example: With a 1,000-token cap, burning 100 can leave room to mint 100 again.
maximum.consequence: The number alone is not a permanent cap if its change permissions remain available.

noMaximum.title: No numerical maximum
noMaximum.body: This removes the numerical supply ceiling. It does not itself give anyone permission to mint; minting and distribution rules still decide how new tokens can be created.
noMaximum.example: A token can have no numerical cap while manual minting remains disabled.

transferable.title: Transfers between holders
transferable.body: Allow holders to send tokens to other identities. This choice is separate from a temporary pause and from permissions for minting, burning or other actions.
transferable.example: A transferable reward can be sent to another member.
transferable.consequence: Transferability cannot change after creation. Non-transferable tokens require protocol 14 or later.

paused.title: Start with transfers paused
paused.body: Start the token with ordinary transfers stopped. Someone needs pause/resume authority to resume them later. Distributions and other configured actions follow their own rules.
paused.example: Prepare an initial allocation, then let the authorized owner resume transfers at launch.

mintRecipient.title: Default new-token recipient
mintRecipient.body: Choose where new tokens go by default. This recipient also receives the initial supply; without a default, the initial supply goes to the contract owner.
mintRecipient.example: Choose a treasury identity to receive both the initial allocation and default future mints.

mintIdentity.title: Recipient identity ID
mintIdentity.body: Enter the complete public identity ID of the intended recipient. A correctly formatted ID does not prove that you control that identity or its signing keys.
mintIdentity.example: Copy your treasury's full identity ID from its identity details.

mintOverride.title: Choose a recipient for each mint
mintOverride.body: Allow an authorized minter to name a recipient for an individual mint instead of using the default. This does not grant minting authority or change the initial allocation.
mintOverride.example: Mint 10 new reward tokens directly to a member instead of the treasury.

allowFrozen.title: Transfers to frozen identities
allowFrozen.body: Choose whether an identity whose token balance is frozen can still receive transfers. Receiving tokens does not remove the freeze or let that identity spend them.
allowFrozen.example: An account can receive a payment while its outgoing transfers remain blocked.

performer.title: Who can perform this action
performer.body: Choose the owner, a specific identity, or a group allowed to carry out this action. No one disables it now, but an administrator may still be able to change that choice.
performer.example: A group may approve mints while a different identity controls changes to that rule.

administrator.title: Who can change this rule
administrator.body: The rule administrator can change the action's permission settings within the selected allowances. This authority is separate from permission to perform the action itself.
administrator.example: If the owner can change the mint rule, a group is not necessarily the final minting authority.

flags.0.title: Allow removing all performers
flags.0.body: Allow the rule administrator to set the action's performer to No one. This constrains a later rule change; it does not give everyone permission to edit the rule.
flags.0.example: The administrator could disable future minting by removing its performer.

flags.1.title: Allow removing all administrators
flags.1.body: Allow the rule administrator to set the administrator to No one. Once no administrator remains, this rule can no longer be updated through that authority.
flags.1.example: Lock the chosen minting authority by removing its rule administrator.

flags.2.title: Allow replacing the administrator
flags.2.body: Allow the current rule administrator to change who administers this rule. This is a permission for an authorized update, not an extra power granted to every holder.
flags.2.example: Move administration of the mint rule from the owner to a governance group.

identity.title: Public identity ID
identity.body: An identity is a Platform account used to own tokens or hold authority. Use its complete public ID. A format check does not establish ownership or access to signing keys.
identity.example: A group member is identified by their public identity ID, not their wallet address.

groups.title: Shared authority through groups
groups.body: A group acts when the total power of approving members reaches its threshold. Creating the group does not grant powers automatically; assign it to the relevant action rules. Group labels and stable draft IDs are local. Review shows the contiguous positions written to the contract; references follow the same members when an unrelated group is removed.
groups.example: Two members with power 1 each and required power 2 must both approve.

groupName.title: Group label
groupName.body: Give the group a useful label for this draft. The contract refers to groups by their positions; a label is not a public identity ID.
groupName.example: Treasury approvers can be your local label for Group 0.

threshold.title: Required approval power
threshold.body: Set the approval power needed for the group to act. It must be positive and reachable using the members' combined power; approvals are weighted rather than counted by people. A group needs at least two different members. Required power and each member’s power must be between 1 and 65,535.
threshold.example: With member powers 2, 1 and 1, a threshold of 3 needs the first member and one other.

weight.title: Member approval power
weight.body: This is how much the member's approval contributes toward the group's required power. Equal powers give members equal weight; a larger number gives that member more influence.
weight.example: Three members with power 1 and required power 2 form a two-of-three group.

mainGroup.title: Main control group
mainGroup.body: Choose which existing group the Main group option refers to. Each action still needs an explicit permission assignment; selecting a main group does not give it every power.
mainGroup.example: Set Treasury approvers as the main group, then assign Main group to minting.

mainChange.title: Who can replace the main group
mainChange.body: Choose who may change the contract's main control group after creation. This selects change authority; it does not create a group or assign all token actions to one.
mainChange.example: Let the owner replace the main group while minting refers to Main group.

history.title: Token history records
history.body: Choose which on-chain token history ledgers to retain. Transfers, freezes, mints, burns, direct-pricing changes and direct purchases have separate switches. These are contract settings, not local privacy controls.
history.example: Retain transfer history so the token's transfer records can be queried.

keywords.title: Search keywords
keywords.body: Keywords help people find the contract. Names marked searchable in Basics are included automatically; additional keywords can add to the registration estimate.
keywords.example: Add education for a learning reward token.

documents.title: Document types
documents.body: Advanced users can define document types in the same contract using a JSON map of names to schemas. This does not create documents or change token balances. Paste a map of document types, not an entire contract. External references are not loaded; use local fragments. Syntax checks do not replace full contract validation during preparation.
documents.example: Define a note type with a required text field limited to 120 characters.
documents.consequence: Valid JSON syntax does not prove that the complete contract will pass Platform validation.

review.title: Review before creating
review.body: Check amounts, recipients, permanent choices, and every performer and administrator. Hidden or disabled sections can retain change permissions. The creation fee comes from the issuer's Platform balance.
review.example: Confirm the maximum-supply rule is locked if you promise a permanent cap.

readiness.title: Issuer readiness
readiness.body: Creation needs the intended network, a funded Platform identity and an available eligible signing key. Draft checks alone do not confirm network acceptance or successful registration.
readiness.example: An identity with only public information cannot sign the creation request.

rule.mint.title: Mint additional tokens
rule.mint.body: Minting creates new tokens within the current supply limit. The authorized actor can mint; the destination settings determine who receives the new tokens.
rule.mint.example: Mint 10 reward tokens when the outstanding supply has room for them.

rule.burn.title: Burn the actor's own tokens
rule.burn.body: Burning removes tokens from the executing identity's own balance and reduces outstanding supply. It does not let the actor take tokens from another holder.
rule.burn.example: Burning 10 from your balance of 100 leaves you with 90.
rule.burn.consequence: Burned tokens are destroyed; burning is not a recoverable transfer.

rule.freeze.title: Freeze one holder
rule.freeze.body: Prevent a particular identity from sending this token. Receiving while frozen is a separate setting, and permission to unfreeze is a separate action rule.
rule.freeze.example: Freeze one account while other holders continue transferring normally.

rule.unfreeze.title: Unfreeze one holder
rule.unfreeze.body: Remove an identity's freeze so it can spend again when the token's other transfer rules permit. Freeze and unfreeze can have different authorized actors.
rule.unfreeze.example: A governance group can unfreeze an account after reviewing the reason for its freeze.

rule.destroy.title: Destroy a frozen balance
rule.destroy.body: Allow the authorized actor to destroy the target identity's entire frozen token balance. This is separate from burning the actor's own tokens and does not select a partial amount.
rule.destroy.example: A frozen balance of 100 is reduced to zero.
rule.destroy.consequence: Unfreezing the identity later does not restore destroyed tokens.

rule.pause.title: Pause or resume transfers
rule.pause.body: Temporarily stop or resume ordinary transfers for all holders. This does not change permanent transferability; other actions and distributions remain subject to their own rules.
rule.pause.example: Pause transfers during an operational issue, then resume them when ready.

rule.cap.title: Change maximum supply
rule.cap.body: Choose who can change the numerical supply ceiling and who can change that permission. A permanent cap needs both selectors set to No one and all three change allowances off.
rule.cap.example: Keep minting available below 10,000 while locking the ceiling at 10,000.

rule.conventions.title: Change display conventions
rule.conventions.body: Allow later changes to naming and decimal conventions. These can affect how clients present token names and amounts, so choose this authority separately from minting or pausing.
rule.conventions.example: An authorized actor could update localized token names.

rule.recurring.title: Change recurring distribution
rule.recurring.body: This authority can enable, change or disable recurring distribution, including its recipient. Turning distribution off in the draft does not remove this permission.
rule.recurring.example: If the owner retains this power, recurring rewards could be enabled after creation.

rule.destination.title: Change the default mint recipient
rule.destination.body: Choose who may change the default identity for newly minted tokens. This controls future destination changes; it does not move tokens already issued.
rule.destination.example: An authorized actor could switch future default mints from the owner to a treasury.

rule.override.title: Change per-mint recipient choice
rule.override.body: Choose who may enable or disable selecting a recipient for each mint. This changes the recipient-choice policy, not who has permission to mint.
rule.override.example: Lock this rule while keeping individual recipient choice permanently enabled.

rule.marketplace.title: Change marketplace trade mode
rule.marketplace.body: Choose who may change the token's marketplace trading settings later. This rule does not put tokens on sale and is separate from ordinary transfers between holders.
rule.marketplace.example: Keep transfers available while marketplace sales remain unavailable.

rule.pricing.title: Change direct-purchase pricing
rule.pricing.body: Choose who may set or change the price used for direct token purchases. Assigning this authority does not set an initial price or make a purchase.
rule.pricing.example: An authorized owner could configure a direct-purchase price later.

distribution.title: Additional token allocations
distribution.body: Recurring, scheduled and once-per-identity distributions provide additional allocations beyond the initial supply. Eligible recipients must claim them; enabling a schedule does not automatically transfer tokens.
distribution.example: A treasury can claim recurring allocations after eligible periods have passed.

recurring.title: Recurring distribution
recurring.body: Allocate tokens over repeated periods using the chosen amount function and recipient. Review its change rule even when this feature starts off; retained authority can enable it later.
recurring.example: A fixed function can allocate 1 token per eligible daily period for the treasury to claim.

scheduled.title: Scheduled distributions
scheduled.body: Set specific dates, recipients and token amounts. A date makes an allocation eligible under the distribution rules; recipients still need to claim it.
scheduled.example: Make 25 tokens available to a treasury on a chosen date.

once.title: Once per identity
once.body: Each eligible identity can claim the configured amount once. One person can control several identities, and available supply can limit claims. This feature requires protocol 14 or later.
once.example: Offer a 1-token allocation per eligible identity, not per person.

interval.title: Repeat interval
interval.body: Set how many time units, epochs or blocks make up one recurring period. The function uses period indices to calculate allocations; the interval does not guarantee an exact claim time.
interval.example: Every 1 day and every 10 blocks describe different kinds of periods.

intervalKind.title: What measures a period
intervalKind.body: Choose elapsed time, Platform epochs, or blocks. Epochs are network accounting periods, and block counts are network progress; neither promises a fixed number of clock hours.
intervalKind.example: Choose time for a daily allowance, or epochs for EvoNode participation allocations.

timeUnit.title: Time unit
timeUnit.body: Time units use fixed durations, not calendar scheduling. Supported intervals must align to whole minutes; a selectable unit alone does not guarantee the chosen interval is valid.
timeUnit.example: The verified one-day interval is 1,440 minutes; one second is not supported.

recipient.title: Distribution recipient
recipient.body: Choose who can receive this allocation. Recurring distribution supports the owner, a specific identity, or EvoNodes by participation; EvoNode allocations require epoch-based intervals.
recipient.example: Use your treasury identity for recurring project rewards.

scheduledDate.title: Scheduled date and time
scheduledDate.body: Choose the local date and time when this allocation becomes eligible. Check the displayed time zone and converted time during review; the recipient must still claim the allocation.
scheduledDate.example: A 09:00 allocation uses the time zone shown beside this form.

onceAmount.title: Amount per identity
onceAmount.body: Enter the number of tokens each eligible identity may claim once. The amount is per identity, not a guaranteed payout to each person, and available supply can limit claims.
onceAmount.example: An amount of 1 gives each eligible identity one 1-token claim.

function.FixedAmount.title: Fixed amount
function.FixedAmount.body: Use the same allocation for every eligible period. Fixed describes the recurring amount, not the token's total supply; supply limits and claims still apply.
function.FixedAmount.example: At 1 token per period, five eligible periods contribute 5 tokens before other restrictions.
function.FixedAmount.formula_note: The same amount at every index.

function.StepDecreasing.title: Step decreasing
function.StepDecreasing.body: Keep an amount for several periods, then reduce it by a chosen fraction. A minimum and a separate trailing amount can shape the later allocations.
function.StepDecreasing.example: The audited example starts 1.00, 1.00, 0.50, 0.50, then 0.25 tokens per index.
function.StepDecreasing.formula_note: Integer division at each decrease; trailing after era 3.

function.Stepwise.title: Stepwise
function.Stepwise.body: Define exact amounts starting at chosen period indices. Each index uses the amount from the latest start reached; setting a later amount to zero stops future emissions.
function.Stepwise.example: Use 0.10 tokens from index 0, 0.05 from index 3, then zero from index 5.
function.Stepwise.formula_note: Use the amount at the latest threshold reached.

function.Linear.title: Linear
function.Linear.body: Increase or decrease the allocation by a steady amount each period, within the chosen bounds. The function's maximum limits each period, not total token supply.
function.Linear.example: The audited example gives 0.10, 0.12, 0.14 tokens, rising to a 0.20-token limit.
function.Linear.formula_note: The maximum limits each interval, not total supply.

function.Polynomial.title: Polynomial
function.Polynomial.body: Shape how fast allocations grow or shrink using a curved pattern. The m/n ratio sets the power, while the offset changes its input. Bounds limit the amount in each period.
function.Polynomial.example: The audited square curve starts 0.01, 0.04, 0.09, then 0.16 tokens.
function.Polynomial.formula_note: The offset is inside the power; this example uses squares.

function.Exponential.title: Exponential
function.Exponential.body: Allocations can grow very quickly with this curve, so check the example and bounds carefully. It uses a natural exponential curve; m/n controls its rate and bounds limit each period’s amount.
function.Exponential.example: The audited example starts 0.10, 0.27, 0.73 tokens, then reaches its 1.00-token maximum.
function.Exponential.formula_note: exp uses base e. The maximum is reached at k = 3.

function.Logarithmic.title: Logarithmic
function.Logarithmic.body: Use a natural logarithm to produce a curve that can rise more slowly over time. The m/n ratio scales the input, and rounding happens before the added amount b.
function.Logarithmic.example: The audited example starts 0.10, 0.16, 0.20, then 0.23 tokens.
function.Logarithmic.formula_note: Natural log; round down before adding b.

function.InvertedLogarithmic.title: Inverted logarithmic
function.InvertedLogarithmic.body: The example allocations fall quickly at first, then more slowly. This curve uses the natural logarithm of a reciprocal input, not one divided by a logarithm.
function.InvertedLogarithmic.example: The audited example starts 0.40, 0.33, 0.29, then 0.26 tokens.

param.a.title: a: scaling coefficient
param.a.body: This whole-number coefficient scales the changing part of the function together with divisor d. It uses the function's base-unit calculation, so it is not an amount entered directly in tokens.
param.a.example: For Linear at 2 decimals, a = 2 and d = 1 add 0.02 tokens per index.

param.b.title: b: added amount
param.b.body: This amount is added to the function's changing part. It is not always the first output because the chosen curve, offsets, rounding and bounds also affect that result.
param.b.example: In the audited logarithmic example, b adds 0.10 tokens after the logarithmic part is rounded.

param.d.title: d: scaling divisor
param.d.body: This positive whole number divides the function's scaled part. It works with coefficient a and the base-unit calculation; it is not a token amount.
param.d.example: For Linear at 2 decimals, a = 2 and d = 2 give a 0.01-token increase per index.

param.m.title: m: ratio numerator
param.m.body: Use m together with denominator n. In Polynomial, m/n is the power; in Exponential it scales the exponent; in the logarithmic functions it scales the input.
param.m.example: In Polynomial, m = 2 and n = 1 select a square curve.

param.n.title: n: ratio denominator
param.n.body: This positive whole number is the denominator paired with m. The pair controls a power or input scale depending on the selected function; it is not a token amount.
param.n.example: In Polynomial, m = 1 and n = 2 select a square-root power.

param.o.title: o: input offset
param.o.body: Shift the period input before applying the curve. This changes the curve's calculation, not the calendar start date, and differs from adding an amount afterward with b.
param.o.example: In the audited square curve, o = 1 makes the input k + 1 before squaring.

param.s.title: s: optional start index
param.s.body: This advanced setting changes the function's period reference. It is not simply a number of days to wait after registration. Leave it blank to use the verified examples' default reference.
param.s.example: The audited recipe tables all leave s blank.

param.initial.title: Initial recurring amount
param.initial.body: This starts the step-decreasing function before its reductions. It is an amount within the recurring formula, separate from the token supply created at registration.
param.initial.example: An initial recurring amount of 1.00 token is held for two indices in the audited example.

param.minimum.title: Minimum per interval
param.minimum.body: This sets a lower bound for the function's regular calculation. Blank means no optional lower bound; zero is an explicit value. Step-decreasing trailing emission is a separate choice.
param.minimum.example: A 0.10-token minimum need not raise a separately configured zero trailing amount.

param.maximum.title: Maximum per interval
param.maximum.body: This bounds the amount calculated for one period. It does not set the maximum outstanding token supply, which is configured separately in Supply & permissions.
param.maximum.example: The linear example stops increasing at 0.20 tokens per index.

param.step_count.title: Intervals per decrease
param.step_count.body: Choose how many period indices share an amount before the next reduction. This is a count of function periods; its clock duration depends on the selected interval.
param.step_count.example: With 2 intervals per decrease, the example uses 1.00 twice, then 0.50 twice.

param.decrease_numerator.title: Reduction fraction numerator
param.decrease_numerator.body: Together with the denominator, this sets the fraction removed at each reduction. It describes the reduction, not the fraction that remains afterward.
param.decrease_numerator.example: A numerator of 1 and denominator of 4 remove one quarter, leaving three quarters.

param.decrease_denominator.title: Reduction fraction denominator
param.decrease_denominator.body: This positive whole number completes the reduction fraction. Each reduction removes that fraction of the previous amount, with integer rounding in the calculation.
param.decrease_denominator.example: A numerator of 1 and denominator of 2 halve the amount at each reduction.

param.maximum_interval_count.title: Maximum reduction era count
param.maximum_interval_count.body: This optional limit counts reduction eras, not individual periods. The trailing amount is used after this era count is exceeded; intervals per decrease determine each era's length.
param.maximum_interval_count.example: With 2 intervals per decrease and a limit of 3, the audited trailing amount starts at index 8.

param.trailing.title: Trailing amount
param.trailing.body: This is the recurring amount used after the step-decreasing era limit is exceeded. It is chosen separately from the normal minimum, so a minimum does not automatically raise it.
param.trailing.example: The audited example settles at 0.10 tokens from index 8 onward.

param.amount.title: Amount per interval
param.amount.body: This is the fixed allocation for each eligible recurring period. Choose tokens or base units in the amount field; the contract stores the equivalent number of smallest units.
param.amount.example: With 2 decimals, 1.00 token corresponds to 100 smallest units.

param.steps.title: Step starts and amounts
param.steps.body: Give each distinct starting index its token amount. The latest start reached selects the amount. Use at least two distinct starts; duplicate indices do not add their amounts together.
param.steps.example: 0: 0.10, 3: 0.05, 5: 0 means 0.10 until index 3, then 0.05 until index 5.

period-index.title: Reading the period index
period-index.body: The index labels a period in the function's calculation. Index zero illustrates the starting boundary; it is not an extra initial-supply payment. Claimable periods follow the network's boundaries.
period-index.example: The tutorial's first five eligible periods use indices 1 through 5.

static-preview.title: Current-parameter preview
static-preview.body: The preview recalculates the current parameters with the selected network protocol. It shows raw units, displayed tokens, and cumulative allocations. The assumed registration reference is explicit; this is an illustration, not a promise of a future claim.
static-preview.example: Changing the linear slope recalculates the table. Index zero is illustrative and is not added to the cumulative allocations.

scheduledAmount.title: Amount for this allocation
scheduledAmount.body: Enter the tokens assigned to this scheduled recipient at this date. This is one allocation, not an amount repeated each period. The recipient must claim it when eligible.
scheduledAmount.example: Assign 25 tokens to the treasury on the chosen date.

permissions.title: Understand the token’s permissions
permissions.body: For each action, inspect who can act, who can change that rule, and the three change allowances. A disabled action can become available later if its administrator retains the necessary authority.
permissions.example: Minting set to No one is not permanently disabled while the owner can change its rule.

fee.title: Estimated creation fee
fee.body: Registration is paid from the issuer identity’s Platform credits; the app can show their DASH equivalent. Keywords and distribution features can affect the estimate. This is not the token’s purchase price.
fee.example: Adding a search keyword can increase the estimated registration cost.

unknownOutcome.title: Registration result is unclear
unknownOutcome.body: A slow or missing response does not prove registration failed. Use Check status to look for the reviewed contract without another payment. Another creation stays blocked while the result is unclear, including after restarting the app.
unknownOutcome.example: If the response is missing, use Check status · no payment to check the same contract.
